text: ChromeOS, a proprietary operating system developed by Google, is derived from the open-source ChromiumOS, which itself originates from Gentoo Linux, and uses the Google Chrome web browser as its primary user interface. Google announced the project in July 2009, initially describing it as a cloud-based operating system where applications and user data reside in the cloud, primarily running web applications. The operating system first shipped with Chromebooks in 2011 and has since been offered as an installable Linux distribution called ChromeOS Flex since 2020. ChromeOS supports progressive web applications, Android apps from Google Play, and Linux applications. In 2025, Google confirmed that ChromeOS will transition from the Linux kernel to the Android kernel, resulting in a merged development path with Android, formally announced at the Snapdragon Summit in September 2025 under the internal codename "Aluminium OS." The new operating system will be desktop-optimized, running the same Android software on both desktop and mobile devices, adapted for different screen sizes, and will support both ARM and x86 processors, with the x86 version expected to be the first mainline maintained x86 architecture version of Android. Jeff Nelson, a Google employee, created the concept of ChromeOS in 2006 as "Google OS," initially a Linux distribution focused on speed, and early versions used Firefox before switching to Chrome in 2007. To determine marketing needs, developers analyzed usage patterns from 200 Google employee machines and their own usage. Google required hardware partners to use solid-state drives for performance and reliability, noting that ChromeOS requires only one-sixtieth the drive space of Windows 7; in 2019, ChromeOS recovery images were still between 1 and 3 GB in size. On November 19, 2009, Google released the source code as the ChromiumOS project, and at a news conference, Sundar Pichai demonstrated an early version that booted in seven seconds and featured a desktop resembling Chrome with application tabs. Chris Kenyon of Canonical announced a contract to contribute engineering resources, and Canonical was an early engineering partner; initially, ChromiumOS could only be built on Ubuntu, but in February 2010, the team switched to Gentoo Linux due to its flexible package management system, and the build environment is no longer restricted to any distribution, though installation guides use Debian (and thus Ubuntu) apt syntax. In 2010, Google released the unbranded Cr-48 Chromebook in a pilot program, with retail hardware delayed until 2011. On May 11, 2011, Google announced two Chromebooks from Acer and Samsung at Google I/O; the Samsung model launched on June 15, 2011, and the Acer model in mid-July. In August 2011, Netflix announced official support for ChromeOS, and later that month, Citrix released a client for remote access to Windows applications. Dublin City University became the first European educational institution to provide Chromebooks to students in September 2011. By 2012, demand for Chromebooks grew, and Google introduced new devices from Samsung, including the first Chromebox, the Samsung Series 3, and a lower-priced Chromebook in October 2012 priced at $250, using an ARM processor from Samsung's Exynos line, with reduced memory and screen resolution; Acer followed with the C7 Chromebook at $199, using an Intel Celeron processor and a laptop hard disk to reduce cost. In April 2012, Google introduced the Aura window manager and a conventional taskbar, marking a shift from a single-browser interface to a more traditional desktop experience. Google Drive integration was added in ChromeOS version 20, released in July 2012, and Adobe Flash support was fully sandboxed by the end of 2012. Before 2013, Google did not manufacture its own ChromeOS devices, which were designed and marketed by third-party partners; this changed in February 2013 with the release of the Chromebook Pixel, which featured an Intel Core i5 processor, a 2,560×1,700 touchscreen, and a price competitive with business laptops. By the end of 2013, analysts were divided on ChromeOS's future, despite predictions of its demise since 2009, as device sales continued to grow. In mid-2014, Time magazine published a piece highlighting conflicting views on Chromebooks' success. Intel's announcement of Intel-based Chromebooks, Chromeboxes, and LG's Chromebase further fueled uncertainty. Seizing the opportunity from the end of Windows XP support, Google offered significant discounts in early 2014 to promote Chromebooks in businesses. ChromeOS devices outsold Apple Macs worldwide in 2020. Since July 2021, ChromeOS's embedded controller has been based on a Google-maintained fork of Zephyr, a real-time operating system. In March 2014, Google hosted a hacking contest called Pwnium, where two exploits were demonstrated and a third at Pwn2Own; all were patched within a week. Google Native Client has been available since 2010, but few apps existed initially; in June 2014, Google announced ChromeOS would sync with Android phones and run Android apps from Google Play, expanding app availability. Google also adopted Material Design, with a new default wallpaper introduced in 2014 and fully integrated in Chrome 117. Chrome Enterprise, launched in 2017, includes ChromeOS, Chrome Browser, and device management features for businesses, offering standard features like bookmark and extension syncing, cloud printing, multi-layered security, remote desktop, and automatic updates, and advanced features such as Active Directory integration, unified endpoint management, advanced security, device policies, guest access, kiosk mode, and app whitelisting/blacklisting. The education sector was an early adopter, and Chromebooks are widely used in classrooms, with cloud-based computing advantages gaining traction in financial services, healthcare, and retail. ICT managers cite benefits such as advanced security, simplified management, reduced operational costs, and secure file access across devices. Google's Grab and Go program allows businesses to provide employees access to fully charged Chromebooks for checkout and return. In February 2014, Google released Chromebox for Meetings, a kit for conference rooms with a Chromebox, camera, noise-cancelling microphone, speakers, and remote control, supporting Google Hangouts, Vidyo, and UberConference. Partners released various models, and in 2016, Google introduced an all-in-one Chromebase for smaller meeting rooms. Google targeted the consumer market with the Chromebook in 2011 and the Chromebook Pixel in 2013, and expanded into enterprise with the Pixelbook in 2017, with a second-generation model released in 2019. In 2021, several vendors offered all-in-one Chromebase devices. Google has partnered with OEMs including Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Samsung; in August 2019, Dell launched the Latitude 5300 2-in-1 Chromebook Enterprise and Latitude 5400 Chromebook Enterprise, designed for security-conscious organizations and bundled with cloud-based support services. Other OEMs like Acer and HP also launched devices with Chrome Enterprise Upgrade. With a broader hardware range, ChromeOS became a viable option for enterprises avoiding migration to Windows 10 before Windows 7 support ended. Laptops running ChromeOS are known as Chromebooks; the first was the CR-48, released to testers in December 2010, with retail models following in May 2011. A desktop design, the Chromebox, was released by Samsung in May 2012, and a partnership with AOPEN led to the first commercial Chromebox in March 2015. In early 2014, LG introduced the first Chromebase, a monitor with built-in camera, microphone, and speakers. The Chromebit is an HDMI dongle that turns a TV or monitor into a personal computer; the first, an Asus model, shipped in November 2015 and reached end of life in November 2020. In March 2018, Acer launched the Chromebook Tab 10, a tablet with a screen size and resolution identical to the Apple iPad and a Wacom-branded stylus that does not require charging. ChromeOS supports multi-monitor setups via video-out ports, USB 3.0 Standard-A, or USB-C, with USB-C being preferred. On February 16, 2022, Google announced a development version of ChromeOS Flex, a distribution that can be installed on conventional PC hardware to replace Windows or macOS, similar to CloudReady, which Google acquired in 2020. ChromeOS automatic updates are available for 10 years for all Chromebooks manufactured in 2019 and onwards, covering the operating system, browser, and hardware; Google maintains a web page detailing the auto-update policy and end dates. Previously, the update period was 8 years, and shorter before that, though earlier models received updates for longer. Initially, ChromeOS was a thin client relying on servers for web applications and data; Google later encouraged developers to create packaged applications using HTML5, CSS, Adobe Shockwave, and JavaScript. In September 2014, Google launched App Runtime for Chrome (ARC), initially with four Android apps—Duolingo, Evernote, Sight Words, and Vine—and in 2016, ARC++ was introduced using Linux kernel features to run Android apps in isolated containers, enabling Google Play availability. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Nougat and Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS (Crostini), allowing desktop Linux applications, which was released to the stable channel in October 2018 as a beta feature.

In 2016, the second version, ARC++, was introduced, using Linux kernel features cgroups and namespaces to create isolated containers that can run Android apps, eliminating the need to recompile apps and enabling access to Google Play for ChromeOS devices. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Android Nougat and Android Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for improved security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS, known as Crostini, allowing desktop Linux applications; this feature was released to the stable channel with Chrome 69 in October 2018 as a beta option and officially released with Chrome 91. All Chromebooks made since 2018, and some earlier models, can run Linux apps, which can be installed and launched alongside other apps. Google maintains a list of devices launched before 2019 that support Linux apps. Since 2013, Linux applications have been run in ChromeOS via Crouton, a third-party script set for distributions like Ubuntu. In 2018, Google officially introduced Crostini, named as a pun on Crouton, which runs a virtual machine via crosvm, using Linux's KVM tool, with the Termina VM containing a Gentoo-based ChromeOS kernel and LXD containers. Linux apps run in isolated containers, not on the VM itself, with a default Debian container and support for installing programs via APT or .deb files, or granting access to files and USB devices. As of ChromeOS 121, Debian 12 (Bookworm) is the default container base image. ChromeOS is built on the Linux kernel, originally based on Ubuntu, changed to Gentoo in February 2010. ChromeOS includes the Chromium Shell ("crosh") with minimal functionality like ping at startup; in developer mode, a full-featured bash shell is accessible via VT-2 or the crosh command shell, with a root password required for full privileges, defaulting to "chronos" or "facepunch" initially, later set to empty. ChromeOS is partially developed under the open-source ChromiumOS project, with ChromeOS receiving only Google and partner support and automatic updates to the latest version. Early in the project, Google shared design goals for ChromeOS, including minimal screen space through a single tab strip, reduced window management, floating "panels" for secondary tasks, and split screens for viewing content side by side, leveraging HTML5 offline modes, background processing, and notifications. On April 10, 2012, ChromeOS offered a choice between a full-screen interface and overlapping, resizable windows via the Ash window manager and Aura graphics engine, including translucent tabs, torn tabs, and a mouse-enabled shortcut list. In 2016, ChromeOS included "Native CUPS Support" as an experimental feature, becoming stable in 2020, enabling most printers even without Google Cloud Print support. Google Cloud Print, which allowed any device to print to supported printers via a proxy installed on ChromeOS, was discontinued after December 31, 2020, and ceased operations on January 1, 2021. ChromeOS stores user files on remote servers, and handling local files offline may cause confusion about which application opens them, a problem noted by Matthew Papakipos as similar to issues in Windows. ChromeOS uses a three-channel release system: Stable, Beta, and Developer (Dev), with a fourth canary channel confirmed by entering the ChromeOS shell in developer mode and using the command update_engine_client -channel canary-channel -update, which requires a powerwash to return to other channels. In 2022, two new channels, LTC (Long-term support candidate) and LTS (Long-term support), were added, available only to Enterprise admins, with LTC providing three months of support before switching to LTS. ChromeOS features a hardened design with auto-updating, sandboxing, and a verified boot process that checks for system compromises, shipped with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and a physical switch under the battery to enable developer mode, which reverses security functions but increases flexibility. Full disk encryption is enabled by default, with the decryption password stored in the TPM, which can be updated manually via settings, resetting the device to factory defaults. The user's Google Account password is the default sign-in method, with additional authentication like PINs, passwords, fingerprint, facial recognition, or smart unlock (via a paired phone) to prevent unauthorized access. If multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled on the Google Account, users may be prompted during setup, with the device designated as "trusted" for subsequent logins, and MFA can be required for each sign-in using hardware tokens like YubiKeys. At its debut, ChromeOS was seen as a competitor to Microsoft Windows and its cloud-based applications, though engineering director Matthew Papakipos argued that ChromeOS is designed for netbooks with limited computational power, unable to run resource-intensive programs like Adobe Photoshop. Some observers, including Tony Bradley of PC World, claimed that existing operating systems like Windows or Linux-based netbooks already provided a web-centric experience similar to ChromeOS, questioning the need for a new system. In 2016, Chromebooks were the most popular computer in the US K–12 education market. In 2020, Chromebooks became the second most-popular end-user operating system, growing from 6.4% in 2019 to 10.8% in 2020, with most growth occurring at the expense of Windows, which fell from 85.4% in 2019 to 80.5% in 2021. Google's offer of multiple open-source operating systems, including Android and ChromeOS, drew criticism, with Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer accusing Google of indecision and Steven Levy noting the dissonance between the two systems at Google I/O 2011.

In 2016, Chromebooks were the most popular computer in the US K–12 education market. In 2020, ChromeOS became the second most-popular end-user oriented operating system, growing from 6.4% in 2019 to 10.8% in 2020, with the majority of growth coming at the expense of Windows, which fell from 85.4% in 2019 to 80.5% in 2021. Google offers several open-source operating systems, including Android and ChromeOS, a setup that has drawn criticism, similar to Apple Inc.'s dual operating systems of macOS and iOS. At the time, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer accused Google of being indecisive. Steven Levy noted that "the dissonance between the two systems was apparent" at Google I/O 2011, where Android's Andy Rubin and Chrome's Sundar Pichai "unconvincingly tried to explain why the systems weren't competitive." Google co-founder Sergey Brin acknowledged that owning two promising operating systems was "a problem that most companies would love to face" and suggested that the two systems "will likely converge over time." This speculation intensified in March 2013 when Sundar Pichai replaced Andy Rubin as senior vice president in charge of Android, placing Pichai in charge of both operating systems. At Google I/O 2014, developers demonstrated native Android software running on ChromeOS via a Native Client-based runtime. In September 2014, Google introduced a beta version of the App Runtime for Chrome (ARC), enabling selected Android applications to run on ChromeOS through a Native Client-based environment without requiring modifications, though some adjustments could improve mouse and keyboard support. At its launch, ChromeOS support was limited to selected Android apps. In October 2015, The Wall Street Journal reported that ChromeOS would be folded into Android to create a single operating system by 2017, with the resulting OS being Android expanded to run on laptops. Google responded by stating that while the company has been working on integrating the best features of both systems, there is no plan to phase out ChromeOS. In 2016, Google enabled full access to Google Play for Android apps on supported ChromeOS devices, replacing the previous Native Client-based solution with a container based on Android Marshmallow that allows direct access to the ChromeOS platform and interaction with Android contracts like sharing. Engineering director Zelidrag Hornung explained that ARC was discontinued due to its limitations, including incompatibility with the Android Native Development Toolkit (NDK) and failure to pass Google's compatibility test suite. On November 18, 2024, Android Authority reported that Google is planning to completely merge ChromeOS into Android.
